Sure—here’s something “free” to read.

Sometimes I think about how a mind is a kind of weather. Thoughts arrive the way clouds do: sometimes slow and luminous, sometimes fast and jagged, sometimes nothing but clear sky for hours. You can’t always tell where a particular storm comes from, and you can’t always stop the rain once it starts. But you can notice patterns. You can learn the difference between a passing drizzle and a season that keeps returning. And you can carry an umbrella.

People talk a lot about control—control your impulses, control your schedule, control your life. But maybe the more interesting goal is calibration: learning what you do when the weather changes. Not the fantasy of stopping every storm, just the ability to dress for it. When you’re tired, you stop negotiating with yourself like it’s a productive meeting. When you’re anxious, you stop pretending you’re calm. You name what’s happening and give it the proper amount of attention, the way you would treat a loud neighbor: not by pretending the sound isn’t there, but by deciding what response actually helps.

There’s another strange thing about weather: it makes you feel differently about distance. Two miles can feel like nothing when the sun is warm. Two miles can feel like an odyssey when the wind is sharp and you’ve forgotten what you came out for. Yet the distance hasn’t changed—only your internal conditions have. That’s true for relationships, too. The same conversation can feel like a bridge one day and a wall the next, depending on what you’re already carrying.

If I could write a small manual for being human, it would be full of gentle instructions:
- Drink water even if you don’t feel like it.
- Eat something even if your appetite has gone on strike.
- Move your body enough to remind it you’re on its side.
- Call one person when you’re lonely, not after loneliness has turned into bitterness.
- Do the boring tasks early, before they become myths in your head.
- Let yourself be a beginner at what scares you.
- And when you can’t fix things, at least choose a small thing you can do.

Maybe none of this “fixes” the world. But it changes the terms of the day. It makes the forecast less frightening because you’re not standing there naked in it. You’re still you—still vulnerable, still temporary—but you’re also resourced. You have habits like shelters. You have language like maps.

And maps don’t remove deserts. They just tell you that a desert is a place you can cross, even if it takes time and water and patience.
